{{Short description|Trick relating differential forms}}
In [[differential geometry]], a branch of [[mathematics]], '''Moser's trick''' (or Moser's argument) is a method to relate two [[differential form]]s <math>\alpha_0</math> and <math>\alpha_1</math> on a [[Differentiable manifold|smooth manifold]] by a [[diffeomorphism]] <math>\psi \in \mathrm{Diff}(M)</math> such that <math>\psi^* \alpha_1 = \alpha_0</math>, provided that one can find a family of [[vector field]]s satisfying a certain [[Ordinary differential equation|ODE]].

More generally, the argument holds for a family <math>\{ \alpha_t \}_{t \in [0,1]}</math> and produce an entire [[Isotopy (topology)|isotopy]] <math>\psi_t</math> such that <math>\psi_t^* \alpha_t = \alpha_0</math>.

It was originally given by [[Jürgen Moser]] in 1965 to check when two [[volume form]]s are equivalent,<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Moser |first=Jürgen |author-link=Jürgen Moser |date=1965 |title=On the volume elements on a manifold |url=https://www.ams.org/tran/1965-120-02/S0002-9947-1965-0182927-5/ |journal=[[Transactions of the American Mathematical Society]] |language=en |volume=120 |issue=2 |pages=286–294 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-1965-0182927-5 |issn=0002-9947 |doi-access=free|url-access=subscription }}</ref> but its main applications are in [[symplectic geometry]]. It is the standard argument for the modern proof of [[Darboux's theorem]], as well as for the proof of [[Weinstein's neighbourhood theorem#Darboux-Moser-Weinstein theorem|Darboux-Weinstein theorem]]<ref name=":13">{{Cite journal |last=Weinstein |first=Alan |author-link=Alan Weinstein |date=1971-06-01 |title=Symplectic manifolds and their lagrangian submanifolds |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/000187087190020X |journal=[[Advances in Mathematics]] |language=en |volume=6 |issue=3 |pages=329–346 |doi=10.1016/0001-8708(71)90020-X |issn=0001-8708 |doi-access=free|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and other [[Normal form (mathematics)|normal form]] results.<ref name=":13"/><ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last=McDuff |first=Dusa |url=https://academic.oup.com/book/43512 |title=Introduction to Symplectic Topology |last2=Salamon |first2=Dietmar |date=2017-06-22 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |isbn=978-0-19-879489-9 |volume=1 |language=en |doi=10.1093/oso/9780198794899.001.0001 |author-link=Dusa McDuff |author-link2=Dietmar Salamon}}</ref><ref name=":02">{{Cite book |last=Cannas Silva |first=Ana |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-540-45330-7 |title=Lectures on Symplectic Geometry |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] |year=2008 |isbn=978-3-540-42195-5 |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-45330-7 |author-link=Ana Cannas da Silva}}</ref>

== General statement ==
<blockquote>Let <math>\{ \omega_t \}_{t \in [0,1]} \subset \Omega^k (M)</math> be a family of differential forms on a compact manifold <math>M</math>. If the ODE <math>\frac{d}{dt} \omega_t + \mathcal{L}_{X_t} \omega_t = 0</math> admits a solution <math>\{ X_t \}_{t \in [0,1]} \subset \mathfrak{X}(M)</math>, then there exists a family <math>\{ \psi_t \}_{t \in [0,1]}</math> of diffeomorphisms of <math>M</math> such that <math>\psi_t^*\omega_t = \omega_0</math> and <math>\psi_0 = \mathrm{id}_M</math>.

In particular, there is a diffeomorphism <math>\psi := \psi_1</math> such that <math>\psi^*\omega_1 = \omega_0</math>.</blockquote>

=== Proof ===
The trick consists in viewing <math>\{ \psi_t \}_{t \in [0,1]}</math> as the flows of a [[Time dependent vector field|time-dependent vector field]], i.e. of a smooth family <math>\{ X_t \}_{t \in [0,1]}</math> of vector fields on <math>M</math>. Using the definition of flow, i.e. <math>\frac{d}{dt} \psi_t = X_t \circ \psi_t</math> for every <math>t \in [0,1]</math>, one obtains from the [[chain rule]] that <math>\frac{d}{dt} (\psi_t^* \omega_t) = \psi_t^* \Big( \frac{d}{dt} \omega_t + \mathcal{L}_{X_t}\omega_t \Big).</math> By hypothesis, one can always find <math>X_t</math> such that <math>\frac{d}{dt} \omega_t + \mathcal{L}_{X_t} \omega_t = 0</math>, hence their flows <math>\psi_t</math> satisfies <math>\psi_t^* \omega_t = \mathrm{const} = \psi_0^* \omega_0 = \omega_0</math>. In particular, as <math>M</math> is compact, this flows exists at <math>t = 1</math>.

== Application to volume forms ==
<blockquote>Let <math>\alpha_0, \alpha_1</math> be two [[volume form]]s on a [[Compact space|compact]] <math>n</math>-dimensional manifold <math>M</math>. Then there exists a diffeomorphism <math>\psi</math> of <math>M</math> such that <math>\psi^*\alpha_1 = \alpha_0</math> if and only if <math>\int_M \alpha_0 = \int_M \alpha_1</math>.<ref name=":2" /></blockquote>

=== Proof ===
One implication holds by the invariance of the integral by diffeomorphisms: <math>\int_M \alpha_0 = \int_M \psi^*\alpha_1 = \int_{\psi(M)} \alpha_1 = \int_M \alpha_1</math>.



For the converse, we apply Moser's trick to the family of volume forms <math>\alpha_t := (1-t) \alpha_0 + t \alpha_1</math>. Since <math>\int_M (\alpha_1 - \alpha_0) = 0</math>, the [[de Rham cohomology class]] <math>[\alpha_0 - \alpha_1] \in H^n_{dR}(M)</math> vanishes, as a consequence of [[Poincaré duality]] and the [[de Rham theorem]]. Then <math>\alpha_1 - \alpha_0 = d\beta</math> for some <math>\beta \in \Omega^{n-1} (M)</math>, hence <math>\alpha_t = \alpha_0 + t d\beta</math>. By Moser's trick, it is enough to solve the following ODE, where we used the [[Cartan's magic formula]], and the fact that <math>\alpha_t</math> is a top-degree form:<math display="block">0 = \frac{d}{dt} \alpha_t + \mathcal{L}_{X_t} \alpha_t = d\beta + d (\iota_{X_t} \alpha_t) + \iota_{X_t} (\cancel{d \alpha_t}) = d (\beta + \iota_{X_t} \alpha_t).</math>However, since <math>\alpha_t</math> is a volume form, i.e. <math display="inline">TM \xrightarrow{\cong} \wedge^{n-1} T^*M, \quad X_t \mapsto \iota_{X_t} \alpha_t</math>, given <math>\beta</math> one can always find <math>X_t</math> such that <math>\beta + \iota_{X_t} \alpha_t = 0</math>.

== Application to symplectic structures ==
In the context of [[symplectic geometry]], the Moser's trick is often presented in the following form.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":02" /><blockquote>Let <math>\{ \omega_t \}_{t \in [0,1]} \subset \Omega^2 (M)</math> be a family of symplectic forms on <math>M</math> such that <math>\frac{d}{dt} \omega_t = d \sigma_t</math>, for <math>\{ \sigma_t \}_{t \in [0,1]} \subset \Omega^1 (M)</math>. Then there exists a family <math>\{ \psi_t \}_{t \in [0,1]}</math> of diffeomorphisms of <math>M</math> such that <math>\psi_t^*\omega_t = \omega_0</math> and <math>\psi_0 = \mathrm{id}_M</math>.</blockquote>

=== Proof ===
In order to apply Moser's trick, we need to solve the following ODE

<math display="block">0 = \frac{d}{dt} \omega_t + \mathcal{L}_{X_t}\omega_t = d \sigma_t + \iota_{X_t} (\cancel{d\omega_t}) + d (\iota_{X_t} \omega_t) = d (\sigma_t + \iota_{X_t} \omega_t),</math>where we used the hypothesis, the [[Cartan's magic formula]], and the fact that <math>\omega_t</math> is closed. However, since <math>\omega_t</math> is non-degenerate, i.e. <math display="inline">TM \xrightarrow{\cong} T^*M, \quad X_t \mapsto \iota_{X_t} \omega_t</math>, given <math>\sigma_t</math> one can always find <math>X_t</math> such that <math>\sigma_t + \iota_{X_t} \omega_t = 0</math>.

=== Corollary ===
<blockquote>Given two symplectic structures <math>\omega_0</math> and <math>\omega_1</math> on <math>M</math> such that <math>(\omega_0)_x = (\omega_1)_x</math> for some point <math>x \in M</math>, there are two neighbourhoods <math>U_0</math> and <math>U_1</math> of <math>x</math> and a diffeomorphism <math>\phi: U_0 \to U_1</math> such that <math>\phi(x) = x</math> and <math>\phi^*\omega_1 = \omega_0</math>.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":02" /></blockquote>This follows by noticing that, by [[Poincaré lemma]], the difference <math>\omega_1 - \omega_0</math> is locally <math>d\sigma</math> for some <math>\sigma \in \Omega^1 (M)</math>; then, shrinking further the neighbourhoods, the result above applied to the family <math>\omega_t := (1-t) \omega_0 + t \omega_1</math> of symplectic structures yields the diffeomorphism <math>\phi := \psi_1</math>.

=== Darboux theorem for symplectic structures ===
The '''[[Darboux's theorem]]''' for symplectic structures states that any point <math>x</math> in a given [[symplectic manifold]] <math>(M,\omega)</math> admits a local [[coordinate chart]] <math>(U, x^1,\ldots,x^n,y^1,\ldots,y^n)</math> such that<math display="block">\omega|_U = \sum_{i=1}^n dx^i \wedge dy^i.</math>While the original proof by [[Jean Gaston Darboux|Darboux]] required a more general statement for 1-forms,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sternberg |first=Shlomo |url=https://archive.org/details/lecturesondiffer0000ster |title=Lectures on Differential Geometry |publisher=[[Prentice Hall]] |year=1964 |isbn=9780828403160 |pages=140–141 |author-link=Shlomo Sternberg}}</ref> Moser's trick provides a straightforward proof. Indeed, choosing any [[symplectic basis]] of the [[symplectic vector space]] <math>(T_x M,\omega_x)</math>, one can always find local coordinates <math>(\tilde{U}, \tilde{x}^1,\ldots,\tilde{x}^n,\tilde{y}^1,\ldots,\tilde{y}^n)</math> such that <math>\omega_x = \sum_{i=i}^n (d\tilde{x}^i \wedge d\tilde{y}^i) |_x</math>. Then it is enough to apply the corollary of Moser's trick discussed above to <math>\omega_0 = \omega |_{\tilde{U}}</math> and <math>\omega_1 = \sum_{i=i}^n d\tilde{x}^i \wedge d\tilde{y}^i</math>, and consider the new coordinates <math>x^i = \tilde{x}^i \circ \phi, y^i = \tilde{y}^i \circ \phi</math>.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":02" />

== Application: Moser stability theorem ==
Moser himself provided an application of his argument for the stability of symplectic structures,<ref name=":2" /> which is known now as '''Moser stability theorem'''.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":02" /><blockquote>Let <math>\{ \omega_t \}_{t \in [0,1]} \subset \Omega^2 (M)</math> a family of symplectic form on <math>M</math> which are [[cohomologous]], i.e. the [[De Rham cohomology class|deRham cohomology class]] <math>[\omega_t] \in H^2_{dR}(M)</math> does not depend on <math>t</math>. Then there exists a family <math>\psi_t</math> of diffeomorphisms of <math>M</math> such that <math>\psi^*\omega_t = \omega_0</math> and <math>\psi_0 = \mathrm{id}_M</math>.</blockquote>

=== Proof ===
It is enough to check that <math display="inline">\frac{d}{dt} \omega_t = d \sigma_t</math>; then the proof follows from the previous [[Moser's trick#Application to symplectic structures|application of Moser's trick to symplectic structures]]. By the cohomologous hypothesis, <math>\omega_t - \omega_0</math> is an exact form, so that also its derivative <math display="inline">\frac{d}{dt} (\omega_t - \omega_0) = \frac{d}{dt} \omega_t</math> is exact for every <math>t</math>. The actual proof that this can be done in a smooth way, i.e. that <math display="inline">\frac{d}{dt} \omega_t = d \sigma_t</math> for a ''smooth'' family of functions <math>\sigma_t</math>, requires some [[algebraic topology]]. One option is to prove it by [[Mathematical induction|induction]], using [[Mayer–Vietoris sequence|Mayer-Vietoris sequences]];<ref name=":3" /> another is to choose a [[Riemannian metric]] and employ [[Hodge theory]].<ref name=":2" />
